prediction_ref.short_label: Agent meta-harness becomes the cross-vendor policy plane for agents by H1 2027

validation_rows.evidence_summary: This fresh June 15 prediction is anchored directly by today's lead: Databricks' June 13 Omnigent open-source meta-harness is the originating event the thesis turns on. Omnigent sits one layer above individual coding agents and agent SDKs, wrapping Claude Code, Codex, Pi, OpenAI Agents and the Claude Agents SDK behind one interface so implementations swap without rewriting. The structurally load-bearing detail the prediction names is where the guardrails live: Omnigent enforces stateful, contextual policy at the meta-harness layer itself, tracking each wrapped agent's actions and applying cost budgets, permissions and OS-level sandboxing across whichever runtime is underneath. That is exactly the relocation the prediction describes - the natural control point for enterprise agent governance moving up from per-runtime configuration scattered across each vendor's harness to a single vendor-neutral layer that brokers, observes and constrains them all. It shipped as a standalone Apache 2.0 OSS project (omnigent-ai/omnigent) timed to the Data + AI Summit rather than a Databricks-only feature, establishing the architectural pattern. What the H1 2027 marker still needs is a second independent vendor or hyperscaler shipping a cross-runtime policy-enforcing meta-harness, or an enterprise-agent governance framework naming the meta-harness layer as the prescribed policy point - neither present on day one, with only the single Databricks instance on the board.

prediction_ref.short_label: Cached-rollout agent fine-tuning reaches a second open framework by H1 2027

validation_rows.evidence_summary: This fresh June 15 prediction is anchored directly by today's local-model lead: the June 12 arXiv paper CacheRL: Multi-Turn Tool-Calling Agents via Cached Rollouts and Hybrid Reward is the originating artifact. CacheRL attacks the most expensive part of teaching a small model to use tools - reinforcement learning over multi-turn tool use normally has to run real tools live thousands of times per training batch - by replaying a three-tier fuzzy cache of past trajectories with token-level masking, paired with a cache-tier-aware hybrid reward that reweights answer quality so the model is not penalized for limitations the cache introduces. The reported numbers are the kind that get a method copied rather than admired: 92% process accuracy on multi-step tool-calling against GPT-5's reported 94%, at roughly 100x less compute, lifting Qwen3-4B-Thinking validation reward from 0.43 to 0.78, with ablations crediting a 17% gain to the cache-aware reward. The structural reason the prediction expects diffusion is that the bottleneck is universal - every team doing agent RL on open models, and the major open post-training libraries (TRL, verl, OpenRLHF, SkyRL, ART, NeMo-RL), pays the same live-tool-execution tax, and cached replay is a drop-in substitution for the rollout phase rather than a new architecture. The H1 2027 marker needs a second mainstream open framework shipping first-class cached-rollout support, or an independent open reproduction on a different base model - today the technique is still confined to the single CacheRL paper and its own repository.

reference_links.label: arXiv - CacheRL: Multi-Turn Tool-Calling Agents via Cached Rollouts and Hybrid Reward

bridge.narrative: The June 12 CacheRL paper is the originating artifact: it removes live tool execution from multi-turn agent RL via three-tier cached-rollout replay plus a cache-aware reward, reporting 92% process accuracy near GPT-5's 94% at ~100x less compute. The bottleneck it cuts is universal and cached replay is a drop-in rollout substitution, the diffusion-prone shape every open post-training library could adopt.
bridge.remaining_gap: Technique confined to the single CacheRL paper and its own repo; no second mainstream framework feature or independent reproduction on another base model yet.
